scope: Primary standards and repository evidence that bound what counters, clocks, signatures, Merkle proofs, and provenance attestations can establish before the RC49 fault outcomes are generated.

confirmedFacts.claim: RFC 9162 defines an ordered binary Merkle tree with SHA-domain separation between leaves and internal nodes, plus inclusion and append-only consistency proofs. These proofs establish membership and prefix consistency of supplied entries; they do not establish that an entry names the correct physical event.
confirmedFacts.resultPeriod: Certificate Transparency Version 2.0 Merkle-tree and proof semantics

confirmedFacts.claim: RFC 9942, published in June 2026, standardizes COSE receipts over verifiable data structures and gives concrete CBOR encodings for RFC9162_SHA256 inclusion and consistency proofs. Verification combines the candidate entry, proof, root, and receipt signature.

RFC 9943, published in June 2026, defines SCITT signed statements and transparent statements. It explicitly states that registration proves a statement was produced by an issuer, not that the statement is accurate, and that log order cannot be assumed to equal issuance order unless the registration policy says so.
confirmedFacts.resultPeriod: SCITT Architecture Standards Track RFC, especially Sections 9.1 and 9.2

confirmedFacts.claim: RFC 8785 supplies a canonical JSON representation for repeatable hashing and signing, while restricting inputs to I-JSON and deterministic property ordering. Canonicalization removes serialization ambiguity but adds no physical-event semantics.

The in-toto project lists the in-toto Attestation Framework v1.0 as its stable attestation format. Its statement/subject/predicate separation is useful for naming evidence, but an application still has to define the predicate that binds a scientific acquisition to a physical event.

SLSA v1.2 is the current approved specification and treats provenance as verifiable information about where, when, and how an artifact was produced. Its software-build threat model informs stage separation, but it does not itself define camera-trigger or wafer-event identity.
confirmedFacts.resultPeriod: SLSA v1.2 approved specification current at review

confirmedFacts.claim: RC48 found no direct X16 frame-identity ledger in three official NIST manifests, a selected DAQ archive central directory, or the X16 hierarchy of the 2025 compilation. The exact count-only class remains C(94736,23), requiring 306 aggregate binary decisions under the ordered-loss model.
confirmedFacts.resultPeriod: RC48 bounded public-provenance audit and exact independent identity-budget calculation

inferences: A valid signature over a Merkle root authenticates a statement about an ordered byte set; it cannot repair a wrong or missing physical-event label already present when the first root was created.
A trigger-allocated counter and a payload commitment answer different questions: the counter contracts event-history ambiguity, while the commitment exposes byte changes after its boundary.
Stage localization requires independently retained boundary commitments. A final counter can reveal an anomalous sequence but cannot say whether capture, export, or packaging caused it.

A clock can replace a counter only within a declared clock domain and error envelope whose entire possible-time interval lies inside one trigger's decision cell. A nominal timestamp field is not sufficient.
Counter reset is not merely another missing record. Unless a signed bridge maps old and new domains, downstream event identities are non-identifiable and the correct action is refusal.
unverifiedProposals: A trigger-domain counter combined with signed Merkle roots at capture, export, and packaging will exactly localize every injected structural fault and every payload mutation occurring after the first commitment.
The same design will correctly abstain on capture-side payload corruption that precedes the first commitment, demonstrating rather than hiding the sensor-boundary limit.

The identity/integrity separation will transfer from camera frames to semiconductor wafer, chamber, recipe, metrology, and maintenance-event lineage when the one-event-to-one-record assumptions are made explicit.

searchStrategy.priority: Standards-track RFCs, official specification sites, primary papers, and official research records. Secondary summaries are excluded from factual claims.
searchStrategy.noveltyBoundary: RC49 does not claim novelty for counters, Ed25519, SHA-256, Merkle trees, signed manifests, transparency receipts, or stage provenance. The testable contribution is the preregistered separation of event identity, byte integrity, stage attribution, clock-domain refusal, and pre-commit observability on one fault corpus.
